etymology: English Puritan divine (1616–1683); from the Welsh patronymic Owen, a form of Eugene, “well-born.”
biblical_def: John Owen was the greatest of the English Puritan theologians, vice-chancellor of Oxford under the Commonwealth, and the most rigorous defender of definite atonement and the doctrines of sovereign grace that the English tongue has produced. His The Death of Death in the Death of Christ (1647) is the standard Reformed treatment of particular redemption: Christ did not die to make all men savable but to save His own; He laid down His life for the sheep, and the sheep are given Him by the Father. Owen pressed the great question that no universal-atonement scheme can answer—did Christ bear the sins of all men, or did He not? If He did, none can perish; if He did not, the atonement is particular by its very nature. His Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers remains the church’s manual for the daily killing of indwelling corruption: “Be killing sin or it will be killing you.” His Communion with God opened the believer’s distinct fellowship with each Person of the Trinity. Owen was a congregationalist in church order, a champion of liberty of conscience under Cromwell, and a pastor who buried ten of his eleven children. The dictionary honors Owen as the model of Reformed exactness joined to experimental godliness, the theologian who showed that the deepest doctrine drives the warmest devotion.
webster_summary: English Puritan divine (1616–1683); supreme defender of definite atonement in The Death of Death and of the believer’s war on sin in The Mortification of Sin.

corruption_summary: Owen is dismissed by modern Arminian and universal-atonement writers as a cold logician, and his demand for the daily mortification of sin is softened into mere self-acceptance.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the caricature of Owen as a man of hard logic without warmth, and the wider modern revolt against definite atonement that his Death of Death answered before it was framed. The universal-redemption scheme—Christ died equally for every man, the difference lying only in man’s response—cannot say what the cross actually accomplished without making it accomplish nothing certain. Owen’s argument stands: an atonement that saves no one in particular saves no one at all. The therapy-age also dilutes his doctrine of mortification, turning the believer’s lifelong killing of indwelling sin into a program of self-acceptance that never names sin as sin.

The principle to recover is Owen’s union of exact doctrine and experimental power. He taught that Christ’s death secured the salvation of His people infallibly, and that the same grace which redeems also sanctifies, so that the believer mortifies sin not to be accepted but because he already is. Doctrine that does not drive the soul to holiness is not Owen’s doctrine; holiness that is not built on sovereign grace is not the gospel.

etymology: English Puritan pastor (1615–1691); Baxter, an occupational surname from the Old English bæcestre, a baker.
biblical_def: Richard Baxter was the Puritan pastor of Kidderminster whose labors transformed a careless town into a praying congregation, and whose The Reformed Pastor (1656) remains the church’s great manual of pastoral diligence—not “reformed” in the doctrinal sense but in the sense of a renewed, watchful ministry that catechizes every family and takes heed to the whole flock. His The Saints’ Everlasting Rest turned the believer’s eye to the heavenly rest that remains for the people of God, and his A Call to the Unconverted pressed sinners with tender urgency. Baxter ministered through plague and civil war, was ejected in the Great Ejection of 1662, and suffered imprisonment under a hostile bench for his nonconformity. Yet the dictionary cannot follow Baxter in all his doctrine. On justification he departed from the Reformed standard into a scheme—later called Baxterianism or neonomianism—that made faith and evangelical obedience a new law whose performance is counted for righteousness, softening the imputed righteousness of Christ that the Reformation recovered. His view of the atonement leaned toward the universal-payment scheme. The dictionary honors Baxter’s pastoral fire and his suffering for conscience while naming his justification error as a real departure from the gospel of grace alone.
webster_summary: English Puritan pastor (1615–1691); author of The Reformed Pastor and The Saints’ Everlasting Rest; honored for pastoral diligence, corrected for his neonomian view of justification.
webster_full: RICHARD BAXTER, Puritan pastor of Kidderminster (1615–1691).
Wrote The Reformed Pastor, the great manual of watchful, catechizing ministry.
Wrote The Saints’ Everlasting Rest, turning the soul to the heavenly rest.
Ejected in 1662 and imprisoned for nonconformity, suffering for conscience.
Held a neonomian view of justification the dictionary names as error.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.

corruption_summary: Baxter’s pastoral writings are rightly loved, but his neonomian doctrine of justification—making faith and obedience a new law counted for righteousness—corrupted the imputed righteousness of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is Baxterianism itself: the scheme that the gospel is a “new law” whose terms are faith and sincere obedience, and that God accepts the believer’s evangelical obedience as his righteousness rather than imputing to him the perfect righteousness of Christ. This softens justification by faith alone into a covenant of milder works, and it confuses the ground of acceptance (Christ’s obedience reckoned ours) with the fruit of it (our obedience flowing from faith). The Reformation recovered that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law; Baxter’s scheme reintroduces the deeds, however refined, into the ground of standing before God.

The principle to recover is the clean Reformed doctrine of justification: Christ’s active and passive obedience imputed to the believer, received by faith alone, apart from any works of our own. Baxter’s pastoral diligence is to be imitated; his justification error is to be refused. A faithful ministry presses men to holiness while resting their whole acceptance on the righteousness of Another.
roots_summary: Puritan pastor of Kidderminster (1615–1691); great on pastoral labor, erring on justification (neonomianism).

etymology: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield (1851–1921), Princeton theologian; Counterfeit Miracles (1918), his lectures defending cessationism.
biblical_def: Benjamin B. Warfield was the great Princeton defender of biblical inerrancy and the clearest modern statement of the cessationist position, set down in his 1918 lectures Counterfeit Miracles. Warfield argued from Scripture and from church history that the miraculous gifts—prophecy, tongues, healings, the working of wonders—were the credentials of the apostles and of those on whom the apostles laid hands, given to authenticate the founding revelation of the New Covenant. The signs of an apostle marked the apostle; when the apostolic age closed and the canon was complete, the sign-gifts that accompanied and confirmed inspired revelation ceased with it. He traced the claimed miracles of later centuries—medieval relics and shrine-cures, Roman canonization wonders, Irvingite tongues, and the faith-healing movements of his own day—and found them counterfeit: not the genuine apostolic gift but credulity, imposture, or the ordinary providence of God misread. Warfield did not deny that God answers prayer or heals according to His will; he denied that the office of miracle-worker and the gift of inspired prophecy continue. The dictionary holds Warfield’s cessationism as the Reformed default: God has spoken finally in His Son, the canon is closed, and the church lives by the sufficient written Word, not by fresh revelations.
webster_summary: B. B. Warfield’s 1918 lectures defending cessationism—the miraculous sign-gifts authenticated the apostolic foundation and ceased with the close of the canon.
webster_full: COUNTERFEIT MIRACLES, B. B. Warfield’s 1918 lectures on the cessation of the sign-gifts.
Argued the miraculous gifts authenticated the apostles and the founding revelation.
The signs of an apostle ceased when the apostolic age and the canon closed.
Examined medieval, Roman, Irvingite, and faith-healing wonders and found them counterfeit.
Holds the Reformed cessationist default: the sufficient written Word, not fresh revelation.

Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,

Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: The charismatic and continuationist movements answer Warfield by claiming the apostolic sign-gifts for the present church; the dictionary holds the cessationist line.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Warfield exposed is the perennial claim that fresh miracles, new prophecy, and revelatory tongues continue—a claim pressed in his day by the faith-healers and revived in the twentieth-century Pentecostal and charismatic movements, the New Apostolic Reformation, and the prophecy conferences of the present hour. The danger is twofold: it sets a private revelation alongside the closed canon, eroding the sufficiency of Scripture, and it loads tender consciences with false promises of guaranteed healing. Warfield’s historical survey showed how readily credulity, suggestion, and outright fraud counterfeit the genuine work of God.

The principle to recover is the finality of revelation in Christ and the sufficiency of the written Word. God who spoke in many parts and many ways by the prophets has spoken last and fully in His Son; the faith was once delivered to the saints. The sign-gifts authenticated that founding deposit and, their purpose served, ceased. The church does not wait on new oracles; she contends for the faith already given.

etymology: Frederick III “the Pious” (1515–1576), Elector of the Palatinate; the title Palatine from the Latin palatinus, of the palace.
biblical_def: Frederick III, called the Pious, was the Elector Palatine who in 1563 commissioned the Heidelberg Catechism, the warmest and most comforting of the Reformed catechisms, and who turned his German territory toward Reformed rather than Lutheran confession. A magistrate converted to a serious and personal Reformed faith, Frederick charged the young theologians Zacharias Ursinus and Caspar Olevianus to draw up a catechism for the churches and schools of his realm, and the result—opening with the unmatched first question, “What is thy only comfort in life and in death? That I with body and soul, both in life and death, am not mine own, but belong unto my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ”—became one of the Three Forms of Unity and a treasure of the whole Reformed church. When summoned before the imperial Diet at Augsburg in 1566 to answer for departing from the Lutheran Augsburg Confession, Frederick refused to recant, declaring that his conscience was bound to the Word of God. The dictionary honors Frederick as a model of the godly magistrate who used his lawful authority not to lord over the church but to provide for the sound instruction of his people, and as the patron under whose hand the Heidelberg Catechism was given to the church.
webster_summary: Elector Palatine (1515–1576) who commissioned the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) and stood unrecanting before the imperial Diet for his Reformed confession.
webster_full: FREDERICK III, ELECTOR PALATINE (1515–1576), called the Pious.
Commissioned the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563 through Ursinus and Olevianus.
Turned the Palatinate from Lutheran toward Reformed confession.
Refused to recant before the Diet of Augsburg in 1566.
A model of the godly magistrate providing sound instruction for his people.
scriptures: Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the secular age denies that a ruler should ever serve the true religion or commend the faith to his people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse that touches Frederick’s memory is the modern assumption that civil authority must be wholly indifferent to truth, so that a magistrate who provides for the sound catechizing of his people is reckoned a tyrant over conscience. Frederick did not coerce faith—faith is the gift of God and cannot be commanded by edict—but he did what a godly ruler may do: he removed hindrances, provided sound teaching, and refused to lend his authority to error. The Reformed two-kingdoms doctrine distinguishes the sword of the magistrate from the keys of the church without pretending the magistrate is an atheist.

The principle to recover is the godly magistrate who, knowing the king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, uses his lawful office to serve the good of his people, including their instruction in the truth, while leaving the conscience bound only to the Word of God. Frederick’s confession before the Diet—that he would not act against Scripture—is the pattern of the ruler who fears God above the emperor.

etymology: Johann Agricola (c. 1494–1566), German Reformer; the Latin surname Agricola, “farmer,” a humanist rendering of his German name Schnitter (reaper).
biblical_def: Johann Agricola was an early associate of Martin Luther who became the chief figure of the first Antinomian Controversy within the Reformation, teaching that the law of God has no place in the life of the Christian and ought not to be preached even to bring the sinner to repentance. Agricola pressed that the gospel alone—not the law—works repentance, and that under grace the moral law is abrogated entirely, so that the believer need not be summoned by the commandments to mortify sin. Luther himself, who had labored to free the conscience from the law as a way of salvation, recognized in Agricola’s teaching a deadly error and answered it in his treatises Against the Antinomians (1539), insisting that the law retains its abiding use: it convicts of sin, restrains the wicked, and guides the believer’s obedience as the rule of a thankful life. The Reformers distinguished the threefold use of the law and refused to set grace against the commandments. The dictionary names Agricola’s antinomianism as a corruption of the gospel of grace—not its flower but its counterfeit—and holds with the Reformers and the 1689 Confession that the believer, though free from the law as a covenant of works, remains under it as the holy rule of obedience.
webster_summary: German Reformer (c. 1494–1566) whose antinomian teaching—that the law has no place in the Christian life—Luther answered as a corruption of the gospel of grace.
webster_full: JOHANN AGRICOLA (c. 1494–1566), early associate of Luther.
Chief figure of the first Antinomian Controversy of the Reformation.
Taught that the law has no place in the Christian life and ought not be preached.
Luther answered him in Against the Antinomians (1539).
Antinomianism is a counterfeit of grace, not its fruit.
scriptures: Rom 3:31
Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law.
Rom 6:1
What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
Rom 6:2

corruption_summary: Antinomianism, ancient and modern, claims that grace abolishes the law in the believer’s life; the Reformers and the 1689 Confession answer that the law remains the rule of a thankful obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is antinomianism itself, the error Agricola first pressed within the Reformation and which has revived in every age that mistakes evangelical liberty for lawlessness. It reasons that since the believer is justified by grace apart from works, the moral law is finished with him altogether—not merely as a covenant of works (which is true) but as a rule of life (which is false). Paul himself raised and crushed the objection: shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? God forbid. To make grace the licence of sin is to overthrow the very holiness grace produces. Sin is the transgression of the law; where the law is silenced, sin is no longer named.

The principle to recover is the threefold use of the law and the Reformed distinction between law as covenant and law as rule. The believer is freed from the law’s curse and its demand as the ground of acceptance, yet established in the law as the holy pattern of the life he now lives by the Spirit. Faith does not make void the law; faith establishes it. The same grace that justifies also teaches the redeemed to deny ungodliness and to walk in the commandments of God.
roots_summary: German Reformer (c. 1494–1566); first antinomian, answered by Luther; the law remains the believer’s rule of obedience.

etymology: Evangelical seminary founded 1924 in Dallas, Texas, by Lewis Sperry Chafer; the institutional home of systematized dispensationalism.
biblical_def: Dallas Theological Seminary, founded in 1924 by Lewis Sperry Chafer, became the principal academic fountainhead of dispensational theology in America and a vigorous defender of biblical inerrancy, expository preaching, and the study of the Greek and Hebrew text. From Dallas came many able teachers and a wide stream of evangelical scholarship; its insistence on the verbal inspiration and authority of Scripture is to be honored, and its rigorous training in the original languages has equipped generations of preachers. Yet the dictionary cannot commend the dispensational system Dallas codified and propagated—the scheme of sharply divided ages, a radical and permanent distinction between Israel and the church as two peoples of God with two destinies, a secret pretribulation rapture, and the rebuilt-temple, restored-sacrifice expectations that flow from it. This dispensational premillennialism is a nineteenth-century novelty traced to John Nelson Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible; it appears in no Reformation confession. The dictionary holds the older covenantal reading: one people of God across both Testaments, the church grafted into the one olive tree, and Christ the substance to whom the whole of Scripture, Moses and the prophets, bears witness. Dallas is honored for its defense of the Word and named for the discontinuity-scheme it spread.
webster_summary: Evangelical seminary (founded 1924) and the academic home of systematized dispensationalism; honored for defending inerrancy, corrected for the dispensational scheme.

corruption_summary: Dispensationalism, systematized at Dallas, divides God’s one people into Israel and the church with separate destinies and reads prophecy through a secret rapture; the covenant reading sees one people of God in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not the seminary’s defense of Scripture but the dispensational system it codified: a scheme of rigidly separated ages, a permanent distinction between Israel and the church as two peoples with two programs, and a secret pretribulation rapture followed by a rebuilt temple and renewed animal sacrifices. This dispensational premillennialism cannot be found in Nicea, in the Reformation confessions, or in the Puritans; it descends from John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and was carried into American evangelicalism by the Scofield Reference Bible. Its sharp wall between Israel and the church runs against the apostle’s word that Christ has made both one and broken down the middle wall of partition.

The principle to recover is the covenantal unity of redemption: one people of God in both Testaments, the church not replacing but being grafted into the believing remnant of Israel, the one olive tree. Christ is the substance to whom Moses and all the prophets pointed; He expounded in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself. The dictionary keeps Dallas’s high view of inspiration and refuses its dividing system.

etymology: The seminary of the Christian Reformed Church in North America, founded 1876 in Grand Rapids, Michigan; named for the Reformer John Calvin.
biblical_def: Calvin Theological Seminary, established in 1876 in Grand Rapids as the theological school of the Christian Reformed Church, stands in the Dutch Reformed tradition shaped by the Three Forms of Unity—the Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Canons of Dort. From its halls and the wider Dutch Reformed stream came the rich heritage of Abraham Kuyper’s vision of Christ’s lordship over every sphere of life, Herman Bavinck’s magisterial Reformed Dogmatics, and the covenantal, confessional theology that has nourished Reformed churches across North America. The seminary has trained ministers to hold fast the form of sound words, to preach the whole counsel of God, and to confess the sovereign grace summarized at Dort—unconditional election, particular redemption, irresistible grace, and the perseverance of the saints. The dictionary honors Calvin Seminary’s confessional Reformed heritage and its labors in catechism and dogmatics, while noting soberly that the Christian Reformed Church, like every modern denomination, has faced the pressure of theological liberalism and the contemporary debates over Scripture’s authority and biblical sexuality; faithfulness in any age is measured by adherence to the Word and the confessions, not by the institution’s name. Where a school holds the standards of Dort and the sufficiency of Scripture, it is to be commended; where it bends to the spirit of the age, it is to be called back.
webster_summary: Seminary of the Christian Reformed Church (founded 1876); heir of the Dutch Reformed tradition of Kuyper, Bavinck, and the Three Forms of Unity.
webster_full: CALVIN THEOLOGICAL SEMINARY, founded 1876 in Grand Rapids, Michigan.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the pressure of theological liberalism on confessional institutions is the live danger to name and resist.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger to name is the slow drift of confessional schools toward theological liberalism—the softening of biblical authority, the renegotiation of creation and human sexuality, the trading of the Three Forms of Unity for the spirit of the age. No seminary is preserved by its founder’s name or its denomination’s history; faithfulness is held, not inherited. The Bereans were commended not for their pedigree but for searching the Scriptures daily to test what they were taught.

The principle to recover is the holding fast of the form of sound words. A Reformed seminary is faithful only as it confesses the sufficiency and authority of Scripture, teaches the sovereign grace summarized at Dort, and equips ministers to convince the gainsayers by sound doctrine. Where Calvin Seminary and the wider Dutch Reformed tradition do this, they are honored; where any institution loosens its grip on the Word, the call is to repentance and return.

etymology: Evangelical network founded 2005 by D. A. Carson and Timothy Keller; commonly abbreviated TGC.
biblical_def: The Gospel Coalition is a broad evangelical network founded in 2005 by D. A. Carson and Timothy Keller to renew the contemporary church in the gospel of Jesus Christ, drawing together pastors and teachers around a Confessional Statement and Theological Vision for Ministry that affirm the inerrancy of Scripture, the sovereignty of God in salvation, justification by faith alone, penal substitutionary atonement, complementarian church order, and the centrality of the gospel for all of life. In its founding documents and much of its publishing the coalition has labored to keep the gospel central, to commend expository preaching, and to gather the soft-Reformed and broadly evangelical streams that some have called the New Calvinism. The dictionary can commend the confessional core where it holds. Yet a coalition is only as faithful as its watchfulness, and the dictionary notes soberly that a broad network gathered around a minimal statement is always exposed to drift—to the pressure of the cultural moment on questions of justice, sexuality, and the boundaries of fellowship—and that two believers may walk together only as they are agreed. The standard is never the platform but the Word. Where TGC keeps the gospel central and the Scriptures sufficient, it is honored; where any voice within it bends the gospel to the age, it is to be tested and, if needful, withstood.
webster_summary: Broad evangelical network (founded 2005) gathered around a gospel-centered, broadly Reformed confessional statement; commended where it holds the core, tested where breadth invites drift.
webster_full: THE GOSPEL COALITION (TGC), founded 2005 by D. A. Carson and Timothy Keller.

A coalition is only as faithful as its watchfulness; the standard is the Word, not the platform.

corruption_summary: A broad coalition around a minimal statement is exposed to the cultural pressures of the age on justice and sexuality; the safeguard is the sufficiency of Scripture, not the breadth of the network.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger to name is the temptation of every broad evangelical coalition: that breadth gathered around a minimal confession opens the door to drift—to the accommodation of the cultural mood on social justice, racial frameworks, and sexuality, and to a unity purchased by silence on points where Scripture speaks. Two can walk together only as they are agreed; a platform that gathers many voices must guard the agreement that alone makes the walking possible. The apostle pronounced even an angel accursed who should preach another gospel; watchfulness is not factiousness but love for the deposit.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency and authority of Scripture as the only standard of fellowship and the gospel as the unmovable center. A coalition serves the church when it keeps the same mind and the same judgment, speaks the same thing, and refuses to trade the offence of the cross for the approval of the age. Where it does this, it is honored; where any voice bends the gospel, it is to be tested by the Word and, if needful, withstood.

etymology: Reformed-charismatic family of churches, formerly Sovereign Grace Ministries (PDI); commonly abbreviated SGC.
biblical_def: Sovereign Grace Churches is a family of congregations, formerly known as People of Destiny International and then Sovereign Grace Ministries, that holds together a Reformed soteriology—salvation by sovereign, electing, particular grace—with a continuationist conviction that the miraculous gifts of the Spirit continue in the church today. In its confession of the doctrines of grace, its emphasis on the cross as the center of the Christian life, and its rich tradition of God-exalting congregational song, SGC has commended much that is good, and its name rightly confesses that salvation is of the Lord from first to last. Yet the dictionary diverges from SGC on two heads. First, on the gifts: the dictionary holds the cessationist position that the revelatory and sign-gifts authenticated the apostolic foundation and ceased with the close of the canon, so that the contemporary practice of prophecy and tongues, however sincere, sets a fallible word alongside the sufficient Scripture. Second, the movement passed through grievous controversy over the handling of abuse allegations and the concentration of authority, a sorrow to be named honestly and not glossed. The dictionary commends SGC’s confession of sovereign grace and its cross-centered worship while holding the cessationist line and pleading for the protection of the flock and the humbling of authority under the Word.

corruption_summary: Continuationism sets a fallible contemporary prophecy alongside the sufficient Scripture, and concentrated authority that fails to protect the flock is a sorrow to name; sovereign grace and the closed canon together are the corrective.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to name is twofold. The first is the continuationist claim that revelatory gifts persist—a claim the dictionary answers with the cessationist conviction that tongues and prophecy were appointed to cease when the canon closed, lest a fallible “word” be set beside the all-sufficient Scripture. The second is the sober history of authority misused: a movement that concentrates oversight and fails to protect the vulnerable wounds the flock Christ purchased with His own blood. Elders are charged to feed the flock willingly, not for filthy lucre, not lording it over the heritage.

The principle to recover is the joining of sovereign grace to the sufficiency of Scripture and the servant-shape of eldership. Salvation is by grace, not of works, that no man should boast; and the same Word that teaches sovereign grace closes the canon and orders the shepherds to guard, not to grasp. SGC’s confession of grace and its cross-centered song are to be received with thanks; its continuationism is to be refused, and its authority humbled under the Chief Shepherd.

etymology: Confessional Presbyterian denomination formed 1973; abbreviated PCA; presbyterian from the Greek presbyteros, elder.
biblical_def: The Presbyterian Church in America is a confessional Presbyterian denomination formed in 1973 by congregations that withdrew from the mainline Southern Presbyterian church (the PCUS) to preserve the historic Reformed faith against the inroads of theological liberalism. The PCA holds the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms as its doctrinal standards, governs by a plurality of elders gathered in graded courts—session, presbytery, and general assembly—and confesses the inerrancy of Scripture, the sovereignty of God in salvation, justification by faith alone, and male-only ordination to the offices of elder and deacon. Its founding watchword set the aim plainly: to be “faithful to the Scriptures, true to the Reformed faith, and obedient to the Great Commission.” The dictionary honors the PCA’s confessional fidelity, its Presbyterian order patterned on the apostolic gathering of apostles and elders, and its stand for the authority of the Word at a cost. As with every living denomination, the PCA must continue to guard its standards against the perennial pressures of the age on worship, sexuality, and the boundaries of office; faithfulness is kept by adherence to the Confession and the Word, generation by generation. Where the PCA holds its standards, it is commended as a faithful Reformed communion.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though every confessional denomination must guard its standards against the age’s pressure on worship, sexuality, and office.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger to name is the same that birthed the PCA: the slow inroad of theological liberalism into a once-confessional body—the loosening of Scripture’s authority, the renegotiation of human sexuality, and the pressure to open the offices of elder and deacon contrary to the Word. The PCA was formed precisely to resist this drift in the mainline church; the resisting is never finished, for each generation must hold what it received. A denomination is preserved not by its founding charter but by faithful courts that hold fast the form of sound words.

The principle to recover and keep is confessional fidelity under the authority of Scripture: elders ordained as Titus was charged to ordain them, matters weighed in the assembly of apostles and elders, all things done decently and in order. The Presbyterian order is not bureaucratic machinery but the apostolic pattern of shepherds gathered to guard the flock. Where the PCA holds the Westminster Standards and the sufficiency of the Word, it is a faithful Reformed communion to be commended.
